unit.title: Develop and apply principles of professional codes of conduct & ethics

summary: This unit teaches you the professional standards expected of a worker in a villa or hotel: what a code of conduct and ethics are, honesty with cash, stock and time, guest confidentiality and privacy, gifts, tips and conflicts of interest, professional boundaries with guests, respect, harassment and discrimination, appearance, punctuality and reliability, reporting wrongdoing, and how to make a sound decision when you face an ethical problem.

blocks.p: Guests give a villa or hotel their money, their privacy and their trust. They leave their passports, cash, phones and laptops in rooms that you clean. They sleep in beds you have made and eat food you have helped to prepare. A skilled worker who cannot be trusted is not a professional. This unit is about **being a worker people can trust**.
It is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees. The standards apply in every job in tourism and in other trades too, and they are the same on the first day as on the last.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks: producing and presenting a staff code of conduct poster for a villa, and role-playing and recording ethical situations. The assessor looks at your reasoning, your tone, and your respect for others.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Codes of conduct, ethics and values

head: Word
What it means
Example
rows: Values
The beliefs about right and wrong that guide how a person behaves
Honesty, respect, fairness, responsibility
Ethics
Knowing right from wrong and choosing to do right, even when it is hard
Handing in found money when nobody saw you find it
Integrity
Being honest and keeping to good principles even when nobody would find out
Telling the supervisor you broke a lamp
Code of conduct
A written set of rules about how staff must behave at a property
'Staff may not accept gifts above J$2,000 without telling the manager'
Policy
The property's rule on one subject
Gifts policy, social media policy
Job description
A document that sets out the duties and tasks of a job
Villa attendant: clean rooms, restock, report faults

blocks.p: A code of conduct is written so that **every worker knows the behaviour that is expected**. A good code is short, clear and fair. It covers honesty, confidentiality, gifts, harassment, appearance, punctuality, alcohol and drugs, social media, safety and how to report a problem.

blocks.h: Learning and following your property's code

flow: Read the code when you start
Ask about anything you do not understand
Sign to say you have read and understood it
Follow it every day
Ask your supervisor when unsure
Help new staff to follow it

blocks.note: The code is not there only to punish. It protects guests, staff and the property, and it protects you, because it tells you clearly what is expected.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: The law as well as the code

blocks.p: Staff must obey the law as well as the property's code. Breaking the law, for example by theft or by selling drugs, can bring fines or arrest, as well as dismissal. Jamaica also has laws that protect workers (for example against harassment and unfair dismissal) and guests' personal information. You do not need to quote sections, but you must know that the law protects people and that the code is not above it.

blocks.h: Why ethics matter in Jamaican tourism

ul: Tourism is a major part of Jamaica's economy, and repeat guests are important.
Word of mouth and online reviews spread fast: one dishonest worker can damage a villa's name.
The Tourism Product Development Company (TPDCo) and the Jamaica Tourist Board promote a high standard of service, and 'Team Jamaica' expects respect for visitors and for each other.
Guests, owners and staff all depend on a property's reputation for honesty and good service.
If you are given too much change, or a shop or a guest pays you too much, **give back the extra** and get a correct receipt.
Record every cash receipt and payment accurately. Never 'borrow' from a cash float, even if you plan to repay it.
Give receipts when you receive money for the property.
Never take advantage of a guest who does not notice an error.
Never take food, drink, toiletries, linen or equipment for yourself without permission, however small.
Do not use the villa's car, boat, tools or phone for personal reasons unless you have clear permission as the policy says.
Treat leftovers according to the property's policy; do not assume they are free to take.
If you break something, tell the supervisor at once and fill in a report. Hiding it makes it worse.
Write the real hours you worked. Putting down 5 p.m. when you left at 3 p.m. is **dishonest**, because the property pays for time not worked.
Sign for only the work you have done. Do not sign a cleaning checklist for rooms you did not clean.
Keep records truthful: do not change or add figures to hide a mistake.
Do not clock in or out for a friend.

flow: Leave guests' belongings where they are
Do not open drawers, bags or cases
If an item is found after check-out, hand it to the supervisor
Record it in the lost property log
Describe it by what you see
Never keep it, however long it has been

blocks.note: Hand in anything you find, from a coin to a phone. The villa's rules say what happens next. A worker who keeps something found 'because nobody will miss it' is a thief.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Everyone makes mistakes. A professional **admits them quickly**, reports them and helps to put them right. A worker who hides a mistake can lose trust, and the cost of the hidden mistake is often bigger than the mistake.

**Confidentiality** means keeping private information secret and sharing it only with the people who need to know. Guests' names, rooms, travel plans, phone numbers, card details, health and personal habits are all private. The law and the property's policies protect them, and Jamaica has a data protection law whose purpose is to protect personal information.

head: Situation
Professional response
rows: A stranger by phone or in person asks if a named guest is staying, or which room or villa
Do not confirm or say anything; politely say you cannot give out guest details; refer to the manager or front desk
Someone asks you for a guest list for a tour or business
Refuse; refer them to the manager
You see medication, letters or documents in a guest's room
Do not read or discuss them; clean around them
A guest's laptop, phone or papers are open
Do not touch them; clean around them with care
A famous guest is staying
Say nothing to anyone; do not take photographs or post anything
Colleagues talk about a guest's health or behaviour at the pool
Stop; private details must not be discussed where others can hear
A guest asks you to keep something secret
Listen politely; if it is a safety or legal matter, you must report it

ul: Do **not** post photographs or details of guests, their villas or their belongings, and do not post 'selfies' with guests unless the guest and the property agree.
Do not post complaints about the property, the guests or colleagues. Use the proper channel.
A team photo from a staff training day is fine if everyone agrees and nothing private is shown.
Remember that anything you post can be copied and shared widely and cannot easily be deleted.
Knock and announce yourself ('Housekeeping') before entering an occupied room, and wait for a reply. If there is a Do Not Disturb sign, do not enter unless the property's rules require a check.
Enter when your work needs it. Leave the door open if you are unsure.
Do not use guests' toilets, towels, phones, bathrooms or beds.
Do not look through bags, wallets or drawers.
Do not talk loudly about guests with other staff in public areas.

blocks.p: Information about co-workers (pay, discipline, health) and about the owner's business (papers, bank details, plans) is private as well. If the villa owner's papers are on a desk, leave them as they are and do not read them.

blocks.note: If you are not sure whether you can share something, assume you cannot and ask your supervisor.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Gifts, tips and conflicts of interest

head: Item
What it is
What to do
rows: Tip (gratuity)
Money a pleased guest gives for good service
Thank the guest. Follow the property's rules: some add a service charge to the bill and share it among staff; some pool tips, others allow staff to keep them
Small gift
A bar of chocolate, flowers, a postcard
Thank the guest; follow the gifts policy, which often asks you to tell your supervisor
Large gift or cash
A large sum or a valuable item
Do not accept without permission. Politely say 'Thank you, I must ask my manager', and tell your supervisor
Bribe
Money or a favour offered to get someone to do something dishonest or unfair
Never accept. Report it

blocks.p: A bribe is not a gift. It is offered to make you do something you should not, such as letting a friend of the guest use the pool without permission, giving a supplier an unfair advantage, or ignoring a rule.
A **conflict of interest** is when your own gain could sway a decision you make at work. Examples:

ul: A taxi driver or tour operator offers you money each time you send guests to him.
You order supplies from a business owned by your cousin without telling your manager.
You have a share in a business that competes with your employer.
You recommend a restaurant because the owner gives you a meal.

flow: Notice the conflict
Do not act on it
Tell your supervisor or manager
Follow their decision
Keep a record of what you told them

blocks.p: The honest answer is not always 'no'. A conflict of interest that is **declared** (told to the manager) can often be managed. A conflict that is **hidden** damages trust. The guest should get honest advice, not the advice that pays you.

blocks.note: If a guest asks you to recommend a tour or a taxi, give your honest advice or the property's approved list, not the one that pays you.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Every guest and co-worker deserves good service and equal respect, whoever they are. **Discrimination** is treating a person unfairly because of their race, colour, religion, sex, age, disability, social class, nationality, sexual orientation or other personal feature.

head: Example
Is it discrimination?
rows: Giving worse service to a guest because of race or accent
Yes
Giving faster service to tourists than to Jamaican guests who pay the same
Yes
Not hiring or promoting someone because of age or religion
Yes
Giving a guest with a disability the help they ask for
No: it is good service
Giving priority to a guest who arrived first
No: it is fair

blocks.p: **Sexual harassment** is unwanted sexual comments, jokes, touching, messages, gestures or requests. It does not matter whether the person doing it is a guest, a co-worker or a supervisor. It is wrong, and Jamaica has a law whose purpose is to protect people from it.

flow: Stay calm and say clearly 'Please stop. That is not acceptable'
Move away or leave the area if needed
Report it to your supervisor or manager at once
Write down what happened, when, where and who saw it
Ask for support; the property should act on the report

ul: You are never to blame for harassment.
If a colleague tells you she is being harassed, listen, support her and help her to report it properly. Do not gossip or laugh it off.
Never harass anyone yourself, including by 'jokes' or messages.

blocks.note: If you ever feel unsafe, leave the room or area, go to a place where there are other people and call the supervisor or security. Your safety comes first.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Be warm and helpful, but keep your relationship professional. **Boundaries** are the limits that keep it that way.

head: Boundary
What you do
rows: Personal phone numbers and social media
Do not give yours, and do not add guests. Use the property's contact details.
Dating and invitations
Thank the guest politely and say that staff do not go out with guests.
Going to guests' rooms or villas off duty
Do not.
Favours that break the rules
Politely refuse, and offer what you may do.
Sharing personal problems
Keep it short and light; do not make a guest your counsellor.
Drinking with guests
Do not drink with guests, on or off duty at the property, as the policy says.

blocks.note: A friendly 'No, thank you, but I hope you enjoy your stay' keeps the relationship warm and professional.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Professional standards: appearance, punctuality and conduct

blocks.p: Your appearance shows guests that you respect them and the standard of the property. Wear your uniform clean and ironed, with a name tag if the property uses one. Keep hair neat and tied back if you handle food or linen, nails short and clean, and personal hygiene good. Wear closed, non-slip shoes. Keep jewellery simple and perfume light.

ul: **Punctuality** is arriving on time and keeping agreed times. A late worker means others must cover for you and guests may wait.
If you will be late (for example, the bus has broken down), **call your supervisor as soon as you can** and say when you expect to arrive. Do not just turn up late or send a message that is not read.
**Reliability** is doing what you said you would do, so that others can depend on you.
If you are ill, tell your supervisor early so that cover can be arranged.

blocks.p: **Accountability** means accepting responsibility for your own actions and mistakes. Say 'I did it, and I will put it right', not 'It was not me.' You are responsible for the accuracy of every record you write and every task you sign for.

head: Rule
Reason
rows: No alcohol or drugs on duty, and do not come to work under their influence
They affect judgement and safety and put guests and co-workers at risk
Do not drink from guests' bars or eat their food
It is theft and a breach of trust
Use your phone only for work during duty, or as the policy allows
Phones distract you and annoy guests
Speak politely; no shouting, swearing or gossip in front of guests
It spoils the guest's stay
Keep to the safety rules
A safe worker keeps guests and colleagues safe
Respect the property: save water and power, sort waste as the villa says
It protects the environment and cuts cost

ul: Share work fairly and help others.
If you disagree with a colleague about how to share the work, talk calmly in private, or ask the supervisor to help.
Do not complain about colleagues in front of guests or on social media.
Give credit to others for good work.

blocks.note: Good standards are shown most clearly when nobody is watching. A professional does the right thing whether or not the supervisor is looking.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Reporting problems and making good decisions

blocks.p: Report anything that harms, or could harm, guests, staff or the property: theft, dishonesty, harassment, unsafe conditions, drugs, or a breach of the code. You may feel awkward when a friend is involved. Even so, if the problem is hidden, guests and staff could be harmed.

flow: Stay calm and write down the facts
Go to your supervisor (or the next person up if the supervisor is involved)
Say what you saw, when and where
Do not accuse or gossip
Keep the matter confidential
Follow up if nothing happens

blocks.p: Someone who reports wrongdoing through the proper channel is sometimes called a **whistleblower**. A good property protects such a person and takes the report seriously.

ol: **Get the facts.** What exactly happened? Who is involved? What is the real problem?
**Check the rules.** What do the code of conduct, the policy and the law say?
**List your options.** What could you do?
**Think about who is affected.** What is the effect on the guest, your colleagues, the property and you?
**Test it.** Would I be happy if my manager and my family knew what I did? Would I be happy to see it in the newspaper?
**Decide and act.** Choose the honest option, even if it is the harder one.
**Report and learn.** Tell the right person and think about how to prevent it happening again.

head: Example
Option that fails
Option that passes
rows: A guest leaves behind US$50 in a checked-out room
Keep it: 'they will not miss it'
Hand it to the supervisor and log it
Co-worker says 'sign my sheet, I will do your rooms tomorrow'
Sign it
Refuse; sign only your own work
A friend asks you to let her use the villa pool while the guests are out
Say yes
Say no; the pool is for guests

head: Who
What can happen
rows: The worker
A warning, suspension or dismissal, as the policy says. For serious acts such as theft, loss of the job and possibly police action. A bad record makes it hard to get another job.
The guest
Loss of property or privacy, distress, an unsafe or unpleasant stay
The villa
Bad reviews, loss of guests and income, legal claims, loss of reputation

flow: Informal talk or advice
Verbal warning
Written warning
Final written warning or suspension
Dismissal

blocks.p: A small breach (for example lateness) usually begins with a **verbal warning**. Serious breaches such as theft or harassment can lead to suspension or dismissal at once, after a fair process. The property must follow its own policy and the law.

ul: I can say what a code of conduct, ethics, values and integrity mean.
I can explain why a villa has a code of conduct and give three rules a code might contain.
I can show honesty with cash, stock, time sheets and guests' belongings.
I can explain why guest confidentiality matters and give four ways to protect it.
I can say what is safe and not safe to post on social media.
I can explain tips, gifts, bribes and conflicts of interest and say what I must do.
I can keep professional boundaries with guests and refuse politely.
I can explain discrimination and sexual harassment and say how to respond and report.
I can show professional standards in appearance, punctuality, reliability and accountability.
I can say what to do when I will be late.
I can report a safety or honesty problem even when a friend is involved.
I can use the steps for an ethical decision.
I can explain the results of breaking the code for the worker, the guest and the villa.
I can say why staff must obey the law as well as the code.

terms: Code of conduct
Written rules on how staff must behave.
Ethics
Knowing right from wrong and choosing to do right.
Values
Beliefs about right and wrong that guide behaviour.
Integrity
Being honest and principled even when nobody would find out.
Confidentiality
Keeping private information secret and sharing it only with those who need to know.
Personal data
Information about a person, such as name, address or card number, that the law protects.
Conflict of interest
When personal gain could sway a work decision.
Bribe
Money or a favour offered to get someone to act dishonestly or unfairly.
Tip (gratuity)
Money a guest gives for good service.
Discrimination
Treating a person unfairly because of race, religion, sex, age, disability or another feature.
Sexual harassment
Unwanted sexual comments, touching or requests.
Boundary
A limit that keeps a relationship professional.
Accountability
Accepting responsibility for your actions and mistakes.
Punctuality
Arriving on time and keeping agreed times.
Reliability
Doing what you said you would do.
Whistleblower
A person who reports wrongdoing through the proper channels.
Verbal warning
The first step in discipline for a small breach.

c1.title: The cleaning checklist at a Treasure Beach villa
c1.text: At a six-bedroom villa in Treasure Beach, attendant Kemar is cleaning with Nadine, who has worked there for years. At 3:00 p.m. Nadine asks Kemar to sign the cleaning checklist for two bedrooms she did not clean because she is tired, and promises to do them first thing tomorrow. Later, Kemar sees Nadine put three bottles of the villa's coconut oil into her bag. The owner, Mr. Grant, is away until Friday.

c2.title: A well-known guest in Port Antonio
c2.text: A well-known cricketer is staying at a villa in Port Antonio. Housekeeper Camille cleans his villa and sees his prescription medicine on the bedside table and an open letter on the desk. In the afternoon, a woman phones and says she is a magazine journalist. She asks which villa the cricketer is in and when he checks out. Later, a co-worker, Troy, wants to post a photo from the pool deck with the cricketer in it on his social media.

c3.title: An offer from a supplier in Mandeville
c3.text: A villa in Mandeville buys its fresh produce from a local market. The villa's store clerk, Winsome, is offered J$20,000 by a new vegetable supplier if she will tell the manager that his prices are the lowest, though they are higher than the current supplier's. The same day, a guest leaves US$30 for the housekeeping team 'for the lovely week', and another guest offers her a gold bracelet as a thank-you gift. The villa has a gifts policy that says all gifts above a small value must be reported.

c4.title: A difficult evening at a Negril villa
c4.text: At a villa in Negril, housekeeper Latoya is turning down a guest's bed in the evening when a male guest follows her into the room, makes comments about her body and puts his hand on her arm. She feels uncomfortable. Later, her supervisor, Mr. Reid, says he 'cannot give her the better shift' unless she goes for a drink with him. In the dining area a waiter, Orane, serves a group of tourists quickly but makes a local couple wait 30 minutes though they came in first.

c5.title: Standards on a busy Saturday in Runaway Bay
c5.text: On a busy Saturday, villa attendant Sasha leaves home early, but her bus breaks down and she will be 40 minutes late. When she arrives she notices that her co-worker, Delroy, smells of rum and is unsteady on his feet. Another co-worker, Paulette, texts a friend during the guests' breakfast. A guest asks Sasha to recommend a tour, and she knows a tour operator who gives staff a small payment for referrals.

questions.q: Nadine asks Kemar to sign the checklist for two bedrooms she has not cleaned. What should he do?
o: Refuse, and sign only for his own work
Sign, because she promises to clean them tomorrow
Sign, but write the time next to his own name
Sign, if she signs for his bedrooms in return
questions.why: Signing for work that was not done is dishonest and makes the record untrue. A professional signs only for what he has done.

questions.q: Why is signing for work that was not done a problem, even if it is done later?
o: It means that Kemar will have to clean the rooms twice
It breaks the villa's rule about wearing a uniform
It takes too long to write the entry in the book
It makes a false record that others rely on
questions.why: The supervisor and guests rely on the record to show the rooms were cleaned. A false signature is a breach of honesty.

questions.q: Kemar sees Nadine put three bottles of the villa's coconut oil in her bag. What is the right action?
o: Say nothing, because it is only a few bottles
Take three bottles himself, so it is fair for all
Report what he saw to the person in charge
Tell all the other staff so that everyone knows
questions.why: Taking stock without permission is theft, however small. Report the facts to the person in charge, without gossip or confrontation.

questions.q: Mr. Grant, the owner, is away until Friday. Who should Kemar tell?
o: Nobody, until Mr. Grant is back on Friday
The manager or supervisor on duty at the villa
Only Nadine, to give her a chance to stop
The guests, so that they can protect their things
questions.why: A report goes to the next person in authority, who can act at once. Waiting or telling the wrong person lets the problem continue.

questions.q: What should Camille do about the medicine and the open letter in the cricketer's villa?
o: Clean around them; do not read or discuss them
Read the letter, in case it needs urgent attention
Tell her friends what medicine the guest takes
Put them in a drawer so that the desk looks neat
questions.why: A guest's medicines and letters are private. Clean around them, do not move or read them, and do not talk about them.

questions.q: How should she answer the caller who says she is a journalist?
o: Say he is at the villa on the hill until Tuesday
Say 'I cannot say' but give his check-out date
Ask the caller to ring back, then give her details
Politely refuse to give out guest details
questions.why: Staff never confirm that a person is staying, or where. Refer the caller to the manager or front desk, who decide what to say.

questions.q: Troy wants to post a photo of the pool deck with the cricketer in it. What is the right response?
o: Post it, but leave out the cricketer's name
Post it, because the cricketer waved at the camera
Do not post it unless guest and villa agree
Post it, if nobody else's face can be seen in it
questions.why: Photographing and posting a guest breaks his privacy and the villa's trust. Always have the guest's and the property's permission first.

questions.q: Camille is proud to work for a famous guest and wants to tell her family. What should she remember?
o: Telling family does not count as sharing information
Who is staying is confidential, whoever the guest is
It is fine if she does not give the name of the villa
Famous people want everyone to know where they are
questions.why: Confidentiality applies to every guest, and information cannot be controlled once it spreads. A casual remark can put a guest at risk.

questions.q: What is the J$20,000 that the new supplier offers Winsome?
o: A bribe, offered to make her act unfairly
A gift, because the supplier is being friendly
A tip, because she works in the store
A reward for good service to the villa
questions.why: Money offered to get someone to do something dishonest or unfair is a bribe. It must be refused and reported.

questions.q: What should Winsome do about the offer?
o: Accept it, but tell the manager the prices are fair
Accept it and give half of it to the manager
Refuse it, but keep quiet about the offer
Refuse it and tell the manager about it
questions.why: A bribe is refused and reported, so that the villa can protect itself. Keeping quiet leaves the villa open to unfair deals.

questions.q: What should the housekeeping team do about the US$30 left by the guest?
o: Share it among themselves and say nothing
Give it all to the most senior attendant
Thank the guest and follow the tips rules
Refuse it, since tips are never allowed anywhere
questions.why: Properties set their own rules: some pool tips, some share a service charge, some let individuals keep them. Follow the policy and be open about it.

questions.q: How should the attendant answer the guest who offers her a gold bracelet?
o: Accept it and wear it for the rest of the shift
Thank him; she must ask her manager first
Accept it quietly, since it is a thank-you
Refuse it sharply, so that he does not offer again
questions.why: A valuable gift needs permission under the gifts policy. A polite 'thank you, I must ask my manager' protects both the worker and the guest.

questions.q: What should Latoya do first when the guest touches her arm and comments on her body?
o: Say clearly 'Please stop' and leave if needed
Laugh it off, so that the guest is not offended
Say nothing and finish turning down the bed
Slap the guest and walk off the property at once
questions.why: Unwanted sexual comments and touching are sexual harassment. Say clearly that it is not acceptable, move away, and then report it. She is not to blame.

questions.q: After leaving the room, what is the right next step?
o: Wait to see whether he does it again
Tell the other guests to avoid that room
Post about it on social media that night
Report it and write down what happened
questions.why: A quick report with a written note of what, when and where lets the property act. A good property takes it seriously.

questions.q: Mr. Reid says she can have the better shift if she has a drink with him. What is this?
o: A friendly invitation from a good boss
A normal decision about who works which shift
Sexual harassment: he is misusing his power
A way of rewarding hard work in the team
questions.why: Using authority to ask for personal favours is harassment. Since her supervisor is the problem, she reports it to the next level of management.

questions.q: What is the waiter, Orane, doing wrong by making the local couple wait 30 minutes?
o: Serving the tables in the order that guests arrived
Giving worse service because of who they are
Giving priority to guests who pay in foreign currency
Protecting the villa's income from its best guests
questions.why: Treating Jamaican guests worse than tourists is unfair discrimination. Every guest deserves equal respect and service in the order they arrived.

questions.q: Sasha's bus has broken down and she will be 40 minutes late. What should she do?
o: Phone her supervisor as soon as she can
Say nothing and come in when the bus is fixed
Ask a friend to tell the supervisor later in the day
Go home and call in sick for the whole day
questions.why: Lateness affects the whole team. A professional tells the supervisor early and says when she will arrive, so cover can be arranged.

questions.q: Delroy smells of rum and is unsteady on his feet. What should Sasha do?
o: Say nothing, because he is her friend
Cover for him by doing his rooms herself
Warn the guests to keep away from him
Tell the supervisor quietly, in private
questions.why: Alcohol affects judgement and safety, and puts guests and colleagues at risk. Report it to the supervisor quietly and factually.

questions.q: Paulette is texting during the guests' breakfast. What is the problem?
o: Nothing, if the phone is on silent
Nothing, because breakfast is quiet anyway
It distracts her and is disrespectful
Only the supervisor is allowed to object
questions.why: Using a phone on duty takes attention from guests and looks unprofessional. Use phones only as the policy allows.

questions.q: The guest asks Sasha to recommend a tour. What is the professional answer?
o: Recommend the operator who pays her a commission
Honest advice or the villa's approved list
Say that staff cannot talk about tours at all
Recommend the cheapest tour, whatever its quality
questions.why: Recommending a tour for her own payment is a conflict of interest. Honest advice or the property's own list serves the guest and keeps trust.
